notes: Borg Olivier's Nationalist Party governs alone (28 of 50 seats since 1966), so there is no real coalition partner; the centre parties of the early 1960s (Christian Workers' Party, Democratic Nationalist Party) dissolved in 1966, and template slot 2 holds an invented liberal-Europeanist professional milieu ('Malta Ewropea'). Labour stays in slot 3 as in MD. Mabel Strickland's Progressive Constitutional Party (Crown and British-connection loyalists) sits in slot 0; the Crown itself (House of Windsor) in 23. Slot 22 switches from the Royal Malta Artillery to the Malta Land Force on 1 Oct 1970 (transfer decided in 1968). No MD sprites exist for this tag.

0.name: Progressive Constitutional Party
0.text:
The Progressive Constitutional Party was founded in 1953 by Mabel Strickland, proprietor of the Times of Malta and daughter of Lord Strickland, the Anglophile prime minister of the inter-war years. Loyal to the British Crown and to the Catholic Church, it held one seat in Parliament from 1962 to 1966 and now survives as a small group of notables around Miss Strickland and her newspapers.

The party regards the British connection as Malta's shield against communism, Mintoff's socialism and economic ruin, and wants the defence agreement and the British bases preserved at almost any price. Many of its sympathisers would prefer firm government under British protection to the bitter feuds of Maltese party politics. Its leverage lies in the Times of Malta and in friends in London and the services.

1.name: Partit Nazzjonalista
1.text:
The Nationalist Party, heir to the nineteenth-century movement for self-government and Italian culture, has governed since 1962 under Prime Minister Giorgio Borg Olivier, who led Malta to independence on 21 September 1964. In the election of March 1966 it won 48 percent and 28 of the 50 seats, and it must face the voters again by 1971.

The party stands for Christian democracy, close ties with the Church, membership of the Commonwealth and the Council of Europe, and a defence agreement that keeps British forces and aid flowing while the economy shifts to tourism and industry. It is negotiating an association with the European Economic Community. Its base lies among the professional classes, devout Catholics, farmers and Gozo, and its leverage rests on government patronage.

2.name: Malta Ewropea
2.text:
European Malta is the outlook of a new professional middle class in Sliema, Valletta and the university: young lawyers, doctors, architects and businessmen who came of age after the Second Vatican Council and the end, in 1969, of the long war between the Church and the Labour Party. They belong to no party, though many vote Nationalist, and they read the English-language press and look to Rome, London and Brussels.

They want Malta to become a modern European state: association with the European Economic Community, civil liberties and press freedom, respect for private conscience in matters such as civil marriage, and an economy open to tourism and foreign investment. Firmly Western, they are weary of clerical politics and class war alike. Their leverage lies in education, wealth and the professions.

3.name: Partit Laburista
3.text:
The Malta Labour Party, founded in 1921 and rebuilt after 1949 by Dom Mintoff, is the main opposition, having won 43 percent and 22 seats in 1966. Mintoff, an architect and prime minister from 1955 to 1958, broke with Britain after the failure of integration and led Labour through years of conflict with the Church, whose sanctions against the party's leaders were lifted only in 1969.

Labour stands for democratic socialism, the welfare state, public control of key services and a Malta free of foreign bases, or properly paid for them. Mintoff wants to renegotiate the defence agreement, tilt toward neutrality and win friends in the Arab world. Its base lies among dockyard and service workers and the harbour towns, and its muscle in the General Workers' Union.

4.name: Partit Komunista Malti
4.text:
The Communist Party of Malta was founded in 1969 at a secret congress in Gwardamangia by left-wing militants who had left the Malta Labour Party after years of struggle for independence. Its general secretary is Anthony Vassallo. Watched by the police and condemned by the Church, it works semi-clandestinely with perhaps a hundred members.

The party follows the Soviet line: it demands the closure of British and NATO installations, strict neutrality, public ownership of the banks and the dockyard, and solidarity with the socialist countries and the Arab liberation movements. It hopes to push Labour leftward and to build a base among dockyard workers and young trade unionists. Its leverage is minimal, but its fraternal ties with the parties of the Eastern bloc give it a foothold.

5.name: Iż-Żgħażagħ Ribelli
5.text:
The Rebel Youth are the Maltese students and young workers touched by the revolt of 1968: undergraduates at the Royal University of Malta, sixth-formers, young Labour activists and dockyard apprentices. They argue in coffee bars and student societies over Vietnam, Paris and Prague, and circulate duplicated sheets that mock both the clerical establishment and the respectable opposition.

They demand the removal of British bases and NATO facilities from Maltese soil, a secular state, an end to censorship, student power in the university and solidarity with liberation movements from Palestine to Vietnam. Mintoff's Labour seems to them too cautious, the Communists too obedient to Moscow. Their leverage lies in their energy and their talent for staging protests on a small island where everyone hears of them.

6.name: Malta Mediterranja
6.text:
Mediterranean Malta is a current of conservative nationalists, merchants and traders with North Africa who argue that Malta's future lies not with Britain or NATO but with its Arab neighbours. They point to the Semitic roots of the Maltese language, the island's historic trade with Tripoli and Tunis, and the revolution of September 1969 in Libya, whose new rulers are demanding the departure of British and American bases.

Socially conservative and devoutly Catholic, they resent British tutelage and the permissive habits brought by tourists and settlers, and want a neutral Malta financed by Arab oil money rather than base rents. They see Colonel Gaddafi as a potential patron. Their leverage lies in commercial ties with Libya and in Labour's own growing interest in the Arab world.

7.name: Il-Mintoffjani
7.text:
The Mintoffians are the hard core of Dom Mintoff's devotees in the dockyard, the General Workers' Union branches and the Labour clubs of the harbour towns. Hardened by the years of interdiction, when Labour activists were denied the sacraments, and by street clashes with Nationalists, they see their leader, Il-Perit, as the only man able to free Malta from Britain, the Church hierarchy and the old families.

They want Labour to win power and keep it: a strong executive unchecked by courts and press, a purge of the establishment, the expulsion of the British forces and close friendship with Nasser's Egypt, Algeria and revolutionary Libya, whose one-party regimes they admire. Their leverage lies in disciplined crowds, union muscle and their readiness to fight for their party in the streets.

8.name: al-Majlis al-Islami al-Shi'i al-A'la
8.text:
The Supreme Islamic Shia Council was created by Lebanese law in 1967 to give Lebanon's Shia their own institutions, and in 1969 Imam Musa al-Sadr, an Iranian-born cleric settled in Tyre, became its chairman. Its reach extends along the Mediterranean trading routes through Lebanese Shia merchants and seamen, a few of whom pass through Valletta's Grand Harbour, where Arabic sounds familiar to Maltese ears.

Sadr preaches a reformist, socially engaged Shia Islam: dignity and development for the poor, coexistence with Christians and resistance to Israeli raids on southern Lebanon, rather than clerical revolution. He seeks friends among Christian clergy and Arab governments alike. In Malta his influence is negligible, but his message of coexistence resonates on a Catholic island at the edge of the Arab world.

9.name: Hizb al-Da'wa al-Islamiyya
9.text:
The Islamic Dawa Party is a clandestine Iraqi Shia movement formed in Najaf in the late 1950s by young clerics and laymen around Ayatollah Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr. Since the Ba'athist regime turned on the Najaf seminaries in 1969, expelling foreign students and arresting clerics, its members face arrest and torture, and some have fled to the Gulf, Lebanon and Europe.

Dawa calls for an Islamic state guided by the Shia jurists, rejecting both Western liberalism and Ba'athist socialism, and builds a disciplined network of secret cells among students, merchants and professionals. It has no organisation in Malta, and its ideas reach the island only through the occasional Iraqi student or seaman. Its strength lies in its discipline and in the prestige of the Najaf clergy.

10.name: al-Tariqa al-Sanusiyya
10.text:
The Senussi Order, the Sufi brotherhood founded in 1837 by Muhammad ibn Ali al-Senussi, gave Libya its royal house: its head, Idris I, reigned as king from 1951 until the officers of Muammar Gaddafi seized power on 1 September 1969. The king is in exile, the crown prince is under arrest, and the new regime treats the order's lodges in Cyrenaica with suspicion.

Its followers stand for a pious, conservative Islam under a hereditary Islamic monarchy friendly to Britain and the United States. Malta, an hour's flight from Tripoli and long a partner of the monarchy, hosts Libyan merchants and royalist exiles who dream of restoration. Their leverage lies in tribal loyalties in Cyrenaica, exile wealth and the sympathy of London and Washington.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani and is banned throughout the Arab world for its attempts to win over army officers. In Libya it has sought followers among students and officers, and its members now watch the new revolutionary regime, itself born of an officers' conspiracy, with hope and suspicion; a few Libyan students carry its pamphlets to Malta.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and every existing Muslim regime, demanding a restored caliphate that would unite the Islamic world against both Western and Soviet power. It renounces armed action for now and concentrates on persuasion and on winning influential supporters. In Malta its leverage is negligible, but its cadres are disciplined and patient.

12.name: Jama'at al-Ikhwan al-Muslimin fi Libya
12.text:
The Libyan Muslim Brotherhood took root after 1949, when the future King Idris gave refuge to Egyptian Brothers fleeing persecution, who taught in Libya's schools and inspired local students to found their own branch. Tolerated under the monarchy, it now faces a revolutionary regime whose young officers admire Nasser, the Brotherhood's persecutor, and distrust any rival source of religious authority.

The Brotherhood preaches Islam as a complete system of faith, law and social order and seeks to Islamise society gradually through education, preaching and charity, rejecting both Arab socialism and communism. Its members are teachers, students and merchants, some of whom trade with or study in Malta. Its leverage lies in its networks in schools and mosques and in its links with the Brotherhood abroad.

13.name: Malta Development Corporation
13.text:
The Malta Development Corporation was set up in 1967 to steer the island's industrialisation as Britain ran down the garrison and naval base that had been the pillars of the economy. Working with the planners of the Office of the Prime Minister and the new Central Bank of Malta, founded in 1968, it builds industrial estates, offers tax holidays and grants, and courts British, German and American manufacturers.

Its technocrats believe that Malta's survival depends on planning, discipline and investment rather than on party rhetoric or the quarrels between Church and Labour. Neutral between the blocs in economic matters, they would welcome any government that let experts run the economy. Their leverage lies in control of factories, grants and jobs at a time of emigration and redundancies.

14.name: Arċidjoċesi ta' Malta
14.text:
The Archdiocese of Malta has been led since 1943 by Archbishop Michael Gonzi, who with the Bishop of Gozo commands the allegiance of an overwhelmingly Catholic people through hundreds of priests, parishes, religious orders, schools and lay associations. In the 1960s the bishops placed sanctions on the Labour leadership and declared it sinful to vote for Labour or read its press; the conflict ended only with an agreement in 1969.

The Church defends Catholic education, the indissolubility of marriage, the censorship of immoral publications and its considerable property, and expects governments to respect its constitutional position. Distrustful of Mintoff yet wary of British Protestant influence, it places the faith above any foreign alliance. Its leverage lies in the pulpit, the confessional, Catholic Action and the feasts of every village.

15.name: National Bank of Malta
15.text:
The National Bank of Malta, founded in 1946 by Maltese merchant and banking families, is the island's leading locally owned bank, alongside the British-owned Barclays. Its directors and shareholders belong to the circle of import houses, property owners and old titled families who have prospered from the services economy, the building boom and the tourism of the 1960s.

This elite favours sound money, low taxes, the free movement of capital and close ties with the sterling area, and fears both Labour's plans for nationalisation and any interference in private business. It looks to the Nationalist government for stability. Its leverage lies in credit, property and the deposits of the middle classes, which make it indispensable to any government's development plans.

16.name: Malta Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Malta Chamber of Commerce, founded in 1848, is the oldest business association on the island, representing the importers, wholesalers, shipping agents and shopkeepers of Valletta and the harbour towns. Malta imports almost everything it consumes, and the Chamber's members have grown rich supplying the British services, the ships in the Grand Harbour and, increasingly, the tourists filling the new hotels.

The Chamber champions free trade, low duties, minimal bureaucracy and the free movement of goods and capital, and opposes import controls, price regulation and state trading. It welcomes association with the European Economic Community and fears the protectionism and nationalisations proposed by Labour. Its leverage lies in its members' control of supply, credit to retailers and easy access to ministers.

17.name: Din l-Art Ħelwa
17.text:
Din l-Art Ħelwa, the National Trust of Malta, was founded in 1965 by citizens alarmed at the destruction of the islands' heritage and landscape; its name, 'this sweet land', comes from the national anthem. Its volunteers restore chapels, towers and fortifications neglected since the military moved out, and campaign against the speculative building spreading over the countryside and coast.

It works alongside the Malta Ornithological Society, founded in 1962, which defends migrating birds against the island's deeply rooted hunting and trapping. The conservationists call for planning laws, protected areas and respect for Malta's baroque and prehistoric heritage. Standing above party and bloc, they draw support from the educated middle class and foreign residents, and their leverage lies in public opinion.

18.name: Għaqda Ġenerali tal-Ħaddiema
18.text:
The General Workers' Union, founded in 1943 by dockyard workers, is Malta's largest trade union, organising the dockyard, the ports, transport, public services and the Maltese employed by the British forces. Closely allied with the Malta Labour Party, it stood with Labour through the conflict with the Church and has fought every wave of redundancies as Britain runs down its bases.

The union stands for full employment, higher wages, workers' participation in management and the protection of Maltese jobs against foreign employers. It looks to non-aligned socialism and solidarity with the Arab world rather than to either superpower, and wants the economy freed from dependence on military spending. Its leverage lies in its mass membership and its power to paralyse the harbour.

19.name: Tarzna tal-Ħaddiema
19.text:
The Workers' Dockyard is a circle of shop stewards, left-wing teachers and Labour intellectuals who believe Malta's largest enterprise should belong to those who work in it. Since 1968 the Malta Drydocks, taken back by the government from the private firm Bailey, have been run on its behalf by the British shipbuilders Swan Hunter, a contract they regard as colonial control in a new form.

They look to Yugoslavia's workers' councils and to Tito's non-alignment as a model: an independent Marxism, neither Soviet nor Western, built on self-management, planning and friendship with the Third World. They want elected workers' councils to run the dockyard and every nationalised industry. Their leverage lies in the dockyard's several thousand workers and in the ear of Labour's more radical leaders.

20.name: Malta għall-Maltin
20.text:
Malta for the Maltese voices the anger of shopkeepers, small builders, ex-servicemen made redundant by the British run-down and young couples priced out of housing. Its target is the wave of 'sixpenny settlers', British and other foreign retirees drawn since the 1960s by a flat tax of sixpence in the pound, who buy villas and flats, push up prices and form expatriate enclaves.

The movement demands an end to the settlers' privileges, priority for Maltese families in housing and jobs, curbs on foreign ownership of land and a fairer share of the tourist boom for ordinary people. It distrusts the old parties and the Anglo-Maltese elite alike. Its leverage lies in popular resentment in the villages and harbour towns, which both major parties are tempted to exploit.

21.name: Italianità
21.text:
Italianità is the nostalgic remnant of the pre-war movement that defended Italian language and culture against British rule. Most of the Nationalists interned in 1940 and deported to Uganda in 1942 were patriots rather than fascists, but a hard core admired Mussolini, and the memory of Carmelo Borg Pisani, executed by the British in 1942 as a spy for Fascist Italy, is still quietly honoured by a few.

Its adherents, ageing lawyers and notables with a handful of young admirers of Italy's Social Movement, reject Anglicisation and dream of an authoritarian, Catholic and Latin Malta. Hostile to Labour, communism and British influence, they have no organisation and no seats. Their leverage is limited to old families, Italian cultural circles and the far right of Sicily.

22.name: Royal Malta Artillery
22.text:
The Royal Malta Artillery, raised in 1889 from older Maltese fencible units, is the senior Maltese regiment of the British Army. Its 1st Regiment has served with the British Army of the Rhine since 1962 and is due home in 1970: Borg Olivier announced in 1968 that it would form the core of Malta's own land force, alongside the territorial King's Own Malta Regiment.

The officer corps is professional, British-trained and loyal to the Crown and the constitution, with no tradition of political intervention. Yet it is the only trained Maltese fighting force, and should the island descend into civil strife between Labour and Nationalists its officers would become the arbiters of order. Their leverage lies in their discipline, their weapons and their British connections.

22.name: Malta Land Force
22.text:
The Malta Land Force became the island's own army on 1 October 1970, when some 500 officers and men of the disbanded Royal Malta Artillery enlisted in it together with Maltese engineers and signallers. Led by Maltese officers schooled in the British Army, it guards the islands' installations, assists the police in emergencies and performs ceremonial duties for the state.

The force is small, professional and loyal to the constitution, with no tradition of political intervention. Yet as Malta's only trained fighting force it would become the arbiter of order should the island fall into civil strife between Labour and Nationalists, or should the British forces withdraw. Its leverage lies in its discipline, its weapons and its monopoly of military expertise.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
The House of Windsor reigns over Malta through Queen Elizabeth II, Queen of Malta since independence in September 1964, represented in Valletta by the Governor-General, Sir Maurice Dorman. The Queen, who lived on the island as a young naval wife between 1949 and 1951, returned for a state visit in November 1967, and the Crown still frames Malta's constitution.

Monarchists see the Crown as the guarantor of stability, of the British connection and of the Commonwealth ties that protect Malta's economy and its emigrants in Britain and Australia. Against Labour's growing republicanism, royalists present the Crown as the barrier to radical experiments. Its leverage lies in the Governor-General's reserve powers, the loyalty of the officer class and the affection of many Maltese.
